newsitem.title: USA: Fund prospectuses tell part of the story.
newsitem.headline: Fund prospectuses tell part of the story.

text.p: Before you invest in any mutual fund, the fund sponsor should send you a prospectus -- a document that includes considerable information about the fund's official investment policy.
Should you read it? Probably -- but don't expect it to tell you everything you need to know about the fund.

For starters, the prospectus will tell you about the fund's fees. The fund's expense ratio shows its annual expenses as a percentage of its assets -- for example, a fund with a 1 percent expense ratio spends $1 of every $100 on expenses.

How much is too much? That depends partly on the fund category. For example, an emerging markets fund may have sizable research expenses, so you might reasonably expect to pay as much as 1.7 percent of your investment in annual fund expenses. Indeed, a fund that is spending more on research in that area might even do a better job.

By contrast, an investment grade bond fund shouldn't cost nearly as much to manage. The difference in returns between two funds with comparable credit quality and average maturities isn't likely to be great.

So why not go with a cheap fund? Example: Vanguard Fixed-Income Short-Term Corporate (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum investment; 6.4 percent recent yield; no-load) invests in short-term investment-grade bonds. The fund may also invest in U.S. government securities, commercial paper, or bank obligations.

Another inexpensive choice from Vanguard: Vanguard Fixed-Income GNMA (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; 7.4 percent recent yield; no-load) invests in Government National Mortgage Association certificates. The fund attempts to maintain an intermediate-term average weighted maturity.
A fund's risks also should be spelled out in the document.

Since lawyers write prospectuses, you can be sure that the description of risks will be extremely detailed. That means you can review all of the worst possible things that can happen when you invest in the fund.
If you're still comfortable holding its shares, that's a sign that you'll be able to stay with the fund through short-term fluctuations that might shake out less-informed investors.

The prospectus will also tell you about a fund's past performance. You can compare those numbers with the performance results of similar funds, which you'll find in those funds' prospectuses, or in outside references such as Morningstar Mutual Funds, available in many libraries.
Another reason to read fund prospectuses is to get an idea of the different types of funds that exist.

For example, if you order prospectuses for five different bond funds, you will see some important differences. One fund might invest up to 10 percent in overseas bonds, while another shuns such holdings altogether. Or a fund might invest in long-term securities whose values fluctuate with interest rates, while its competitor sticks to short-term bonds.

Differences in credit quality also are common even within the same category: One investment grade bond fund might invest only in AAA-rated securities, while another can buy a modest slug of high-yield, low-quality bonds.

Equity fund prospectuses will sometimes spell out stylistic differences between funds. You might learn that one manager prefers to buy shares of firms whose profits are rising sharply, while another focuses on slow-growth, asset-rich companies.

Once you've read a few prospectuses, you'll get a sense of what to expect -- and what not to expect. For example, the prospectus may not tell you much about the fund's current investments or the manager's general investment philosophy. Reading the most recent annual report might help -- and the best fund managers typically pride themselves on clearly explaining their strategy to shareholders.

Beyond that, Morningstar can help with a review of the fund's historical performance, recent strategy and current outlook. If you're willing to part with a few dollars to get still better information on a smaller universe of funds, consider the No-Load Fund Analyst (510-254-9017; $225 for 12 monthly issues and annual guidebook).
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
